He Bought a Chevy Corvette for $137,000, Drove 562 Miles, Sold for $99,500
25 photos
Photo: Cars and Bids
Depreciation is a killer, and it affects luxury and sports cars most, unless they are rare, exclusive models. The owner of this 2025 Chevrolet Corvette E-Ray convertible learned it the hard way. He paid $136,890 to drive it off the showroom floor. One year and 572 miles later, he sold it for $37,000 under the sticker.
The original owner bought this Chevrolet Corvette E-Ray 3LZ convertible back in August 2025 and was planning to have fun with it. However life happened and here it is, hardly broken in and already sold. He chose Arctic White for the exterior and Jet Black with contrasting Adrenaline Red stitching and Torch Red seatbelts for the interior. The cabin is sheltered by a power retractable hardtop.
The one-year-old Chevy Corvette rides on five-spoke wheels finished in black, measuring 20 inches up front and 21 inches out back, hiding red-painted brake calipers. The car features the very much appreciated front-axle lift system with memory function for peace of mind when coming across speed bumps and sits on the Magnetic Selective Ride Control.
Photo: Cars and Bids The E-Ray was the first hybrid Corvette with all-wheel drive ever to see the light of day. In the meantime, General Motors pulled the plug on it to make room for the Corvette Grand Sport X, which comes with the brand-new 6.7-liter V8. But the E-Ray is powered by the 6.2-liter LT2 V8 and an electric motor.
Together, they push 655 horsepower (664 metric horsepower) and 595 pound-feet (807 Newton meters) of torque. That is enough to make the hybrid Corvette flash from 0 to 60 mph (0 to 97 kph) in 2.5 seconds, run the quarter mile in 10.5 seconds with a trap speed of 130 mph (209 kph) and max out at 183 mph (295 kph).
An eight-speed automatic transmission puts the power down through all four corners. A tiny 1.9-kWh battery stores enough energy for a very short drive of 3 to 4 miles (5 to 6.5 kilometers) on electric power only.
However, the original owner didn't even get to enjoy much of that performance. After one year and three months, he listed the Corvette for sale with just 562 miles (905 kilometers) on the clock. However, it does make sense. He has a family of four and two "fun cars." With two kids having "too much going on," he is not left with much time to drive the two-seater.
Photo: Cars and Bids So he already got rid of it. For $99,500, which is roughly $37,000 under the sticker, the buyer is getting a very low-mileage car, two key fobs, the manuals, the window sticker, the trickle charger, and a serialized crystal glass model. The Carfax report shows a clean history and no mileage discrepancies. No surprise there! The 'Vette hasn't even required service yet. Steal or deal? What do you think?

By Alex Lennane
13 November 2026
Perishables shippers have limited room to absorb rising airfreight costs, airlines have warned, raising questions over how long some products can remain commercially viable to fly.
While booming demand for AI infrastructure supports higher freight spending, flower and fruit exporters face a harder ceiling: what consumers will pay for their products.
“Perishables are a very low-margin business, in which there is only so much the consumers will pay,” Fred Ruggiero, Cathay Cargo’s VP cargo for the Americas, told The Loadstar at TIACA’s Air Cargo Forum in Miami.
Avianca Cargo CEO Diogo Elias highlighted the difference between customers shipping AI servers and “paying whatever”, and flower exporters with much less scope to accommodate higher transport charges.
He pointed to WorldACD figures showing Latin American yield increases of around 7% to 8%, against 24% to 25% globally, illustrating the region’s difficulty passing on higher fuel costs.
Atlas Air chief commercial officer Martin Drew warned that sustained cost increases could eventually push some commodities out of airfreight.
“The longer it continues, what you start to worry about is … price elasticity, where you get to a point where it’s just no longer viable to send by air cargo,” he said, citing some perishable products as potentially vulnerable to modal shift.
Yet sea is not always an option. For seasonal produce, a delayed harvest can eliminate the time available for an ocean journey, leaving exporters needing airfreight precisely when their plans have become harder to execute.
“As a result of the weather, the harvest may be delayed. That means it’s going to miss the fast boats, so more has to be transported by air,” said Mr Ruggiero.
For Cathay, getting South American cherries to Asian consumers involves coordinating capacity across several carriers and gateways.
“Transporting cherries from Chile through Miami, Los Angeles, or New York and onward to Asia is a complex journey where speed and temperature control are essential,” he explained. “The product needs to move quickly, remaining at the optimal temperature throughout the journey. Otherwise, you’re left with an awful lot of cherry juice.”
Those movements are organised well ahead of the harvest, with interline charter capacity feeding Cathay’s network.
“We have charters lined up with interline carriers from Chile to Miami or Chile to Mexico, so we can get them out to Asia,” said Mr Ruggiero. “The problem is, if it’s all planned in advance and everybody is ready to go, what happens if the crop gets delayed? There’s a lot of communication involved amongst ourselves, the forwarders, the growers, and even down to the farmers.”
One air cargo executive described the precarious economics of a business in which a year’s work could be threatened by rain at the wrong moment, adding: “I don’t think I’d ever want to be in that business.”
Securing lift is another challenge. Cathay reported capacity shortages both from Asia to the US and within Asia.
“So we’re trying to secure additional capacity within the region,” said Mr Ruggiero.
Once space is booked, the handling requirements leave little room for improvisation. Treating all fresh produce alike can undermine the value of an expensive air journey.
“On the handling side, it takes expertise to handle perishables properly, and every type of perishable is handled slightly differently,” he said. “For example: how cold they can be, how much humidity they can withstand, and whether they can be covered or not.”
For forwarders, that means managing several moving targets – the harvest, connecting flights, handling conditions, and a freight bill the customer can afford. A delayed crop can require a faster journey, but it does not necessarily give the grower more money to pay for one.

By Charlotte Goldstone
13 November 2026
Following the Democrats’ midterm US election victories, freight forwarders and importers could face greater stability in trade policy, but little immediate relief from existing duties.
Nunzio De Filipis, co-CEO of CargoTrans, told The Loadstar Podcast the election result could slow the pace of tariff changes, although he expects the duties to remain.
“I don’t think we’re going to see the lever being pushed as fast as it has been,” he said, adding: “But I don’t see them going away.”
He pointed to the survival of Section 301 tariffs on Chinese goods through successive administrations, noting that President Joe Biden had retained and expanded measures introduced during Donald Trump’s first term.
Reuters reported this month that Democratic control of Congress would provide greater opportunities to scrutinise President Trump’s trade agenda, but noted that lawmakers faced significant obstacles to repealing tariffs, including presidential veto powers and existing executive trade authority.
Similarly, the legislative and regulatory advisory arm of professional services firm EY explained in its recent trade policy alert that Democratic control would shift congressional committee leadership and increase oversight of trade policy.
However, the advisory noted that the election result would not itself change the tariffs or presidential trade powers, while substantial legislative changes would still require sufficient Congressional support ,and either President Trump’s signature or a veto-proof majority.
For Mr De Filipis, however, the bigger development could be a shift towards stricter customs enforcement. He suggested that tougher enforcement could attract bipartisan political support, particularly where it protects customs revenue and businesses complying with import regulations.
“I think we will start to see 2027 really be the year of enforcement,” he said, and warned that importers were already experiencing increased audits and requests for information, with customs authorities increasingly leveraging technology to examine trade data more efficiently.
Meanwhile, industry consultant Samantha Jones raised concerns about the wider economic implications of Democratic control, particularly for business investment, consumer spending, and freight demand.
She suggested that potential increases in corporate taxation or regulatory costs could encourage businesses to reduce investment, hiring, and wage growth, although the policies ultimately pursued remained uncertain.
“One potential risk I see is that higher corporate taxes or additional regulatory costs could encourage businesses to become more conservative with their budgets,” she said.
She also highlighted the importance of AI infrastructure investment to manufacturing, construction, and freight volumes, warning that additional regulatory obstacles could slow development.
According to Ms Jones, economic growth has increasingly benefited from technology-intensive industries, meaning strong headline economic figures do not necessarily translate into broader freight demand.
Her concerns extend to household purchasing power, with persistent inflation and slower wage growth potentially weighing on consumer spending and, consequently, demand for goods transportation.

Second-Generation Dacia Spring Is a Complete Revamp of an EV That Has Taken Europe by Storm
25 photos
Photo: Dacia
If one is allowed to call a vehicle low-cost, then the Dacia Spring would be the definition of that. With a price of under 18,000 euros (almost $20,000 at today’s exchange rates) and decent performance for people in the market for a small city car, the Romanian brand’s entry-level vehicle is about to become even more enticing, now that the second generation is here.
Having entered the market back in 2021 as a sort of remake of the Renault City K-ZE (Renault is Dacia’s mother company), packing a Chinese-made electric powertrain, along with body and underpinnings used on several Chinese models, the Spring proved too hard to resist for no less than 210,00 European buyers in some 40 countries.
Back in March, Dacia presented its strategy leading into the next decade, and as part of that it announced that it will release no less than four all-electric vehicles by 2030, a major change of direction for a brand that has until recently focused exclusively on internal combustion engine models.
The first of the four Romanian EVs is the second generation of the Spring, which was presented this week as the freshest offering in the A segment. As Dacia itself says, the only thing it has in common with its predecessor is the name.
Photo: Dacia For the newcomer, Dacia completely shifted direction and opted to build it on Renault's new RG-EV small platform, which is also used on the likes of the E-Tech Twingo and 5, among others. What this did, first and foremost, was to widen the body of the small four-wheeler by seven inches (18 cm).
The platform supports a new electric powertrain and an optimized battery pack. Dacia does not specifically say if this hardware is made in-house or sourced from elsewhere, but it did reveal what they are capable of.
The car's electric motor is good for 80 horsepower and 175 Nm of torque, more than enough for a small city car, and punchy enough to accelerate the Spring from zero to 62 mph in 12.1 seconds, on the way to a top speed of 81 mph (130 kph).
The motor draws power from a 27.5 kWh usable capacity LFP battery, which can store enough electricity to keep the car going for as many as 155 miles (250 km), as measured under the WLTP combined cycle. That's more than enough for the needs of people going for such a small car, which, as per Dacia's own claims, in the first-generation form, covered just 21 miles (34 km) per day on average.
Photo: Dacia As standard, the new Dacia Spring is fitted with a 6.6 kW AC onboard charger that allows the car to be plugged into a domestic socket. It's painfully slow, though, as it needs nine hours to get the Spring from 15 to 80 percent capacity.
Dacia will offer people the option of going for a heavy-duty socket, which cuts the charging times for the same interval to five hours and 40 minutes, or a seven kW wallbox that brings that even lower, at almost three hours.
Finally, there is also a fast charge solution comprising an 11 kW AC charger and 50 kW DC charger, which brings charging times down to almost two hours and 28 minutes, respectively.
There will be several trim levels on the table (Dacia hasn't detailed them all), each with its own particularities. The Journey, for instance, throws in a hands-free card, a reversing camera, and the Media Nav Live system that brings along a 10.1-inch central touchscreen and wireless smartphone mirroring via Apple CarPlay or Android Auto. The Expression version, on the other hand, is equipped with a multimedia system with steering wheel controls.
Photo: Dacia No matter the trim level, the new Dacia Spring throws in a seven-inch instrument panel screen, automatic electric parking brake, and reversing sensors. There are two wheel choices on the table, coming it at 15- and 16 inches.
As for colors, the fresh bodywork of the vehicle can be had in one of four hues, Agave, Schist Grey, Diamond Black, and Glacier White, while the interior will only go for a bluish shade for the upholstery, with Agave accents here and there.
Unlike most other cars Dacia makes, which are produced in Romania, the new Dacia Spring will originate from the company's factory in Novo Mesto, Slovenia . The company did not say when we are to expect the city car to become available to customers.
Pricing for it is also a mystery at the time of writing, but not really, if you think about it. The carmaker is likely to keep the price as low as possible, as this is the only way it can fight entry-level Chinese cars, so don't be surprised if we'll still be dealing with a sticker reading under or around $20,000. We'll be on the lookout for that bit of info and let you know once we learn more.

Ford Expedition Tremor: Project Overland Is the Ultimate Off-Road-Ready Family SUV
17 photos
Photo: Ford From the Road
Meet the Ford Expedition Tremor: Project Overland. It is a one-off custom overlanding concept build that came out of the hands of Ford and Fox Factory Vehicles engineers. The build, which previews potential future factory-backed off-road packages, will make its public debut at the 2026 Los Angeles Auto Show later this month.
Ford is well aware that off-road enthusiasts always come up with something for their off-road-ready SUV, which is a work in progress for its entire life. Sometimes, it’s a couple of extra inches. Other times, it’s about a winch or beefier tires.
That is exactly what the Ford Expedition -based project is all about. Ford and Fox Factory Vehicles outfitted the three-row SUV with heavy-duty trail and recovery gear to mimic an enthusiast-built overland rig. It comes with a 2-inch lift kit, featuring FOX 2.0 Performance Series Coilovers, which raise the ground clearance above the stock Tremor’s 10.6 inches.
The concept SUV wears a unique Tremor graphics scheme with Electric Spice orange accents. Custom leather covers the seats. Those at the front are embossed with the "Expedition Tremor: Project Overland" logo.
Photo: Ford From the Road The Ford Expedition Tremor: Project Overland SUV rides on 17-inch beadlock-capable F-150 Raptor R wheels with BFGoodrich All-Terrain T/A KO2 tires, making sure that no terrain is too rough and the outdoorsy families can keep on exploring, without having to turn around and drive back home if the going gets tough.
A modular F-150 Tremor front bumper houses an integrated hidden WARN winch mount. TRED Pro recovery boards with quick-release pins and heat-resistant black hi-hat paint are mounted for deep mud or sand.
The SUV is powered by the stock 3.5-liter EcoBoost V6, which pushes out 440 horsepower. The V6 has remained unchanged, but the team installed an upgraded intercooler to maintain airflow and cooling behind the winch-equipped bumper and make room for the added accessories.
RIGID Phoenix ditch and roof lights plus DC scene lights illuminate the most remote trails. These accessories are wired to an overhead console with F-150 Tremor upfitter switches and wireless controls.
Photo: Ford From the Road To support multi-day road trips, the concept comes with a full suite of overland shelter and cabin features. A Yakima LockNLoad HD softshell rooftop tent and an OverNOut awning are part of the plan, and so are the custom liftgate side curtains, which attach to the open split tailgate for extra wind and rain protection.
The Project Overland remains a concept vehicle for now and won’t go into production. Ford and Fox Factory are just gauging potential customer demand for a factory-backed, purpose-built overlanding SUV or a future Ford Custom Garage package.
Most of the off-road accessories, including the Yakima tent, awning, RIGID lights, and recovery boards, are already available through Ford’s parts and accessories catalog because there is something that every off-roader already knows, Ford claims: almost nobody leaves a rig stock.

SME forwarders looking to enter pharmaceutical logistics should avoid competing directly with multinationals and instead focus on building specialist capabilities, says Pharma.Aero secretary general Frank van Gelder.
Rising demand from clinical trials and time-critical healthcare shipments, together with the emergence of advanced therapies, is creating opportunities for SMEs, but Mr van Gelder said operators must demonstrate the requisite expertise, systems quality and dependability.
He told The Loadstar : “SME forwarders should become indispensable specialists. The opportunities are in clinical trials, time-critical healthcare, advanced therapies, specialised regional corridors and high-touch services around research centres and hospitals.
“An SME can combine local knowledge, quick decision-making and trusted international partners. Emerging connections with Chinese and Indian innovation ecosystems can create further possibilities, provided operators build real expertise rather than simply market a new lane.”
But he warned forwarders off entering the pharma market simply because of the prospect of attractive margins. GDP compliance, qualified personnel, validated procedures, and temperature-control competence were needed to form the foundations of any operation.
Going further, he noted certification alone was not demonstrative of an understanding of the requirements of different pharmaceutical products, with conventional medicines, clinical trial shipments, and personalised therapies presenting a fundamentally divergent set of challenges.
Mr van Gelder added: “Agility without discipline is not resilience, it is risk. The winning combination is systems, specialist knowledge, human adaptability, and trusted partnerships. Collaboration is essential because no one company controls the full patient-critical chain.
“The future is not necessarily about who owns the biggest network, it is about who can orchestrate the most reliable one. Do not compete on price alone. Compete on expertise, reliability, flexibility, and trust.”
This, he added, included an ability to respond to disruption, which offered SMEs a way to distinguish themselves. Mr van Gelder argued that experienced and empowered teams could sometimes adapt faster than larger organisations with slower governance structures.

ObesityWeek 2026, which kicks off on Saturday, will spotlight presentations on the ascendant amylin pathway, as well as therapies looking to improve the quality of weight loss and patients’ persistence on treatment.
From Nov. 14 through 17, some of the country’s leading weight loss experts and biopharma companies with metabolic assets will gather in Washington, DC, for this year’s ObesityWeek , the annual scientific congress run by The Obesity Society.
“Heading into ObesityWeek, the giants Novo and Lilly will be mainly continuing to roll out their messaging as their challengers, both large and small, strive to gain attention with new or updated data from their pipeline contenders,” Jennifer Lilla, senior operations director at the market research firm CardioVascular Resource Group, told BioSpace over email.
Lilla is particularly excited about the next generation of offerings, many of which aim to improve the quality of weight loss and patients’ persistence on treatment. “Obesity Week is increasingly filled with novel preclinical and early clinical data, some of which represent potential up-and-coming mechanisms,” she said, pointing to emerging pathways to control weight, such as myostatin modulation and ALK7 inhibition .
“Poster sessions are often lively and data-rich, and ObesityWeek 2026 looks to be the same,” Lilla continued.
Of all the emerging pathways, “the next hot target” in obesity is amylin, as BMO Capital Markets’ Evan Seigerman said during a BioSpace webinar in September. While the currently dominant GLP-1 drugs—such as Novo’s Wegovy and Eli Lilly’s Zepbound—are effective, they don’t work equally for everyone and can carry tolerability issues such as nausea, vomiting, constipation and other gastrointestinal side effects.
In contrast, many experts believe that amylin could offer a safer alternative while also providing treatment options to more patients and helping others break through weight-loss plateaus.
Obesity
Should amylin have been obesity therapeutics’ primary target from the start?
While GLP-1 medicines have become synonymous with weight loss, at least one expert thinks amylin would have been the go-to target if biopharma had been focused on the blockbuster indication 10 years ago. A new wave of therapies is now exploring this potentially gentler mechanism.
October 19, 2026
·
5 min read
·

Read more
“GLP-1s changed everything. And nothing,” Antoine Pivron, vice president of Withings Health Solutions, said in an email interview. While the drug class brought impressive weight loss numbers, the industry has now started to look for more, he continued, pointing to other key metrics such as how much of the weight lost is due to fat versus muscle.
“Weight was always the easiest signal to capture, not the most important one,” Pivron said.
These themes will take center stage at ObesityWeek .
Powerhouses face off in amylin arena
Novo will arrive at ObesityWeek with posthoc analyses of the Phase 3 REDEFINE 1 study, scheduled from Saturday through Monday, looking at the physical and psychosocial effects of CagriSema, as well as zeroing in on certain patient populations based on baseline body mass index and complications, Rodman & Renshaw told investors in an Oct. 28 note.
REDEFINE 1 tested CagriSema—a two-drug combo consisting of GLP-1 drug semaglutide and amylin analog cagrilintide—in patients with obesity or who are overweight and also have at least one weight-related comorbidity. REDEFINE 1 primarily assessed patients’ relative change in body weight and the percentage of participants achieving at least a 5% reduction in body weight.
Data released in December 2024 showed an average weight loss of 22.7% at 68 weeks in CagriSema-treated patients versus 11.8% and 16.1% in comparators given cagrilintide or semaglutide alone, respectively. Those on placebo lost 2.3% of their weight at this time point.
Despite the superior weight loss, investors were expecting weight reduction on CagriSema to hit 25% and were thus underwhelmed by these findings, sending the pharma’s shares down more than 20% the day of the readout.
Obesity
Novo Nosedives on Underwhelming CagriSema Phase III Weight-Loss Data
Investors appeared disappointed by CagriSema’s Phase III readout, which showed weight loss that fell short of Novo Nordisk’s prior projections for the therapy. Meanwhile, Eli Lilly’s stock rose on the news.
December 20, 2024
·
3 min read
·
Tristan Manalac
Read more
Also bringing amylin data to ObesityWeek is Lilly, which is working on an asset called EloraTZP that combines the pharma’s GLP-1/GIP dual agonist tirzepatide with the amylin analog eloralintide.
On Saturday evening, the pharma will present preclinical data for this combo, demonstrating that in rats induced to have obesity, eloralintide used alongside tirzepatide resulted in stronger suppression of food intake than either drug given alone.
But Lilly has also generated clinical data for EloraTZP. Phase 2b data in September demonstrated average weight loss of up to 23.3% at 48 weeks in patients on EloraTZP, as compared with 14.8% with tirzepatide and 3% with placebo. Aside from hitting the primary endpoint of superior weight reduction over placebo, EloraTZP likewise led to better sugar control than tirzepatide alone or placebo.
This efficacy , however, came with safety tradeoffs. Across all EloraTZP doses tested, 10.8% to 27% of patients dropped out due to adverse events, versus 0% to 10.8% across different doses of eloralintide alone. Tirzepatide monotherapy and placebo had respective dropout rates of 2.9% and 16.7%.
Advancing a seemingly more tolerable amylin option are Roche and Zealand Pharma, which are collaborating on petrelintide. The partners in March touted “placebo-like tolerability” for petrelintide in the Phase 2 ZUPREME-1 study , with 4.8% of patients treated with the highest dose of petrelintide dropping out due to side effects, as compared with 4.9% for those on placebo.
But while the investigational drug was well tolerated, its efficacy results left analysts disappointed. The April readout presented weight loss data at 48 weeks, showing a 10.7% average reduction in the petrelintide group versus 1.7% in placebo.
Roche and Zealand will present posthoc subgroup analyses of ZUPREME-1 on Sunday afternoon at ObesityWeek, as well as results from a study that co-administered petrelintide with the pharma’s GLP-1/GIP dual agonist eniceptide.
“The amylin class will sort along a frontier of efficacy against tolerability,” Rodman & Renshaw wrote on Oct. 28. “Lilly sits at the high end of both which suggests a population willing to accept higher discontinuation for more weight loss, while petrelintide’s placebo-like tolerability positions it for patients who stop incretin therapy due to nausea and GI disturbance.”
Novo’s edge, meanwhile, is time, the firm said. The Danish powerhouse is closest to market, with a potential FDA approval for CagriSema as early as the fourth quarter. If approved, Novo “will set the first regulatory and pricing reference for the class before either Lilly or Roche reaches their respective Phase 3 readout,” Rodman & Renshaw said.
Obesity
Roche insists amylin obesity drug still valuable for patients who ‘don’t want side effects’
Roche and Zealand Pharma announced last month that their amylin analog petrelintide elicited a 9% placebo-controlled weight reduction at 42 weeks—falling far below analyst and investor expectations.
April 23, 2026
·
2 min read
·
Tristan Manalac
Read more
Quality, persistence as key battlegrounds
“Amylin is the science story. Weight loss quality is the real story,” said Withings’ Pivron.
On Saturday evening, Biohaven will present Phase 2 data for its myostatin/activin pathway inhibitor taldefgrobep alfa, an investigational therapy designed to reduce body weight while preserving lean muscle. Biohaven in March completed enrollment into a Phase 2 study of taldefgrobep alfa, testing weekly and monthly doses of the drug versus placebo in patients with obesity or who are overweight, looking primarily at the total change in weight over 24 weeks. Fat mass and lean mass are secondary endpoints.
There have been no data reveals yet from this mid-stage study, but Peter Ackerman, senior vice president of clinical development at Biohaven, told BioSpace in June that taldefgrobep alfa is meant to overcome the loss of lean muscle, a common stumbling block of GLP-1 therapies.
“If you can shut down both the myostatin and activin signaling pathway, we believe that you can optimize lean mass growth and optimize the reduction in fat mass,” he said. “We believe that we can bring higher quality of weight loss.”

Biohaven looks to obesity to bounce back from run of clinical and regulatory failures

Also presenting muscle-preservation data at ObesityWeek is Wave Life Sciences, according to an Oct. 28 note from Leerink Partners. Wave is working on the siRNA therapeutic WVE-007, which is designed to knock down the INHBE protein. Loss-of-function mutations in the gene encoding INHBE have been linked to better body composition. Wave’s presentation is scheduled for Sunday afternoon.
Wave will present interim Phase 1 data from the Phase 1/2a INLIGHT study at ObesityWeek. A readout in March showed that a 240-mg dose of the drug resulted in a 14.3% reduction in visceral fat at six months—a significant improvement from baseline. Participants receiving that dose saw a 5.3% drop in total fat and a 2.4% increase in lean muscle at that timepoint. In the higher 400-mg group, however, participants lost just 5% visceral fat and 1% of total fat, while also losing 0.2% lean mass. Wave’s shares crashed 54% in the wake of the data drop.
But these preliminary weight loss figures aren’t the trial’s primary endpoint, according to a clinical trials database. Rather, the main goal of the study was to demonstrate WVE-007’s safety. Wave said that WVE-007 was generally safe and well tolerated across treatment groups, including the even higher 600 mg dose, with no treatment discontinuations or serious treatment emergent adverse events.
Wave’s presentation at ObesityWeek “could provide an opportunity to share the 600 mg Phase 1 data expected in 4Q26,” Leerink wrote on Oct. 28. Findings from the Phase 2a portion of INLIGHT are expected by next year.
Aside from weight loss quality, Pivron contended that treatment persistence is also a crucial metric that is increasingly attracting attention. “Across the industry, roughly half of patients are gone within six months,” he said.“The question used to be ‘how fast can we hit the weight-loss target?’ Now it’s ‘do results hold, and are we reducing total cost of care or just adding a new cost line?’”
On this front, Leerink pointed to Rhythm Pharmaceuticals, which is set to present final Phase 3 data for its melanocortin 4 receptor agonist Imcivree (setmelanotide) on Monday afternoon in acquired hypothalamic obesity. Imcivree was approved for this indication in March, supported by data from the late-stage TRANSCEND trial, which found an 18.4% placebo-adjusted reduction in body mass index at 52 weeks.
“The 2-year data should provide greater clarity on the durability of treatment benefit, long-term safety and tolerability, and treatment persistence,” the firm said in its note. All of these “are critical to assessing setmelanotide’s long-term commercial potential.”

Cleveland-Cliffs Chairman and CEO Lourenco Goncalves speaks at the company’s Middletown Works steel plant in Ohio on Aug. 21, 2026. U.S. Vice-President JD Vance and other Republican leaders attended the event marking a planned $1-billion investment. Credit: Facebook
Posted By: Henry Lazenby November 13, 2026
Cleveland-Cliffs (NYSE: CLF) faces possible court action from Ottawa over layoffs at Stelco, as U.S. tariffs and the shift of auto production south test Canada’s ability to protect manufacturing jobs.
The Ohio-based steelmaker has temporarily laid off 175 workers in Hamilton and denies breaching its takeover commitments. Industry Minister Mélanie Joly has warned that Ottawa could seek court-ordered compliance, penalties or a forced sale of Stelco.
“I bought Stelco because I could not afford anymore having Stelco flooding the market here in the United States to the detriment of my own company,” Cliffs chairman and CEO Lourenco Goncalves told CBC TV on Oct. 27. “Stelco has a very good cost structure and could be making a lot more margin and employing a lot more people.”
Goncalves presented a successful Stelco as an opportunity for Canada as well as Cliffs, arguing that its use of U.S. iron ore made the two countries’ steel industries interdependent.
For Canadian miners, the stakes extend from iron ore and zinc used in steel to nickel, lithium and graphite intended for batteries. Ottawa’s effort to keep more processing and manufacturing at home depends on factories buying those materials. Stellantis’ (NYSE: STLA) proposed sale of its Brampton assembly plant to defence manufacturer Roshel offers exposure to another market, but its capacity to replace lost auto jobs and demand remains uncertain.
Tariff squeeze
Cliffs bought Stelco in November 2024 in a deal announced at $3.4 billion (US$2.5 billion), including debt. Ottawa approved it with five-year commitments to maintain unionized employment, retain most salaried staff and honour collective agreements and pension obligations.
Trump’s steel tariff doubled to 50% in June 2025, raising the cost of serving U.S. customers from Canada. Cliffs supports that protection while advocating a common North American barrier against outside suppliers. It wants Ottawa to curb imports of galvanized steel, coated with zinc to resist corrosion.
The company has idled cold-rolled and coated finishing operations in Hamilton, about 70 km southwest of Toronto. Goncalves blamed an oversupplied Canadian galvanized-steel market, while saying stronger hot-rolled prices had helped make Stelco a positive contributor to third-quarter earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization.
Overall Stelco production would be maintained by concentrating on hot-rolled products, he said in the company’s quarterly results release. The cuts nevertheless reduce the finishing work performed in Canada before steel reaches customers.
Cliffs shares closed 0.2% stronger at US$13.10 in New York on Thursday, following a 2.2% gain the previous day.
Production moves south
Stellantis illustrates the broader contest for manufacturing. The carmaker’s U.S. expansion, announced in October 2025, envisages US$13 billion of investment over four years, a 50% increase in annual vehicle production and more than 5,000 additional jobs. The plan includes reopening Belvidere, Illinois, for Jeep Cherokee and Compass production.
Production of the Compass had been earmarked for Brampton. Instead, Roshel agreed on Monday to acquire the plant and associated equipment for an undisclosed amount. The sale agreement is expected to close by year-end, subject to conditions and regulatory requirements.
Ottawa knew of the potential sale months before Prime Minister Mark Carney condemned it as a betrayal of workers. Federal officials had been engaged regularly since August, CBC News reported Wednesday, citing a source with direct knowledge. Citing three sources, CTV News reported Tuesday that Ottawa took part in the talks and did not stand in the way.
Joly’s office denied that she negotiated or endorsed the deal. Her role was to help resolve the dispute between Stellantis and Unifor, and she had not met Roshel, spokesperson Mathis Denis told The Canadian Press on Wednesday.
About 2,200 Unifor members have been on indefinite layoff at Brampton. Ottawa and Ontario pledged up to $529 million and $513 million, respectively, in 2022 for a broader investment program involving Brampton, Windsor and research centres. The retreat tests subsidy conditions as well as labour agreements.
Joly was scheduled to meet Stellantis, Unifor and Ontario representatives Thursday. Stellantis has offered to repay government support received for Brampton’s original retooling plan, without disclosing the amount, The Canadian Press reported.
The contrast with Stellantis’ U.S. expansion shows the challenge facing Canada: a tariff-protected American market can attract production that Canadian governments had counted on retaining. Softer EV demand and changes in vehicle strategy are also reshaping investment decisions.
Battery plans shrink
Honda Motor (NYSE: HMC) indefinitely suspended its planned $15-billion Ontario EV and battery complex in May, following an earlier two-year postponement. The planned chain included vehicle assembly, batteries and components, tying the auto expansion to Canada’s ambitions in mineral processing.
Honda’s existing Canadian operations continue. On Monday, it announced a $166-million investment in Alliston for hybrid and gasoline vehicle production, part of a broader $867-million commitment including future spending and related expenses. It said the investment would maintain a workforce of more than 4,000.

CHARLOTTE, N.C. — Nuclear verdicts against trucking companies rarely grow out of the facts of the crash itself, according to trucking defense attorney Doug Marcello. Plaintiff attorneys look for evidence of systemic failure, and Marcello said AI-only dash cams are giving them a new place to find it: risky driving the camera recorded but the AI never flagged.
That leaves fleets answering for footage their safety teams never coached. Marcello, a shareholder at Saxton & Stump, made the case at the American Trucking Associations’ Management Conference & Exhibition in Charlotte, North Carolina, on a panel with Sean Ritchie, a vice president at Solera Fleet Solutions. Solera, which sells video safety systems with a human review layer.
The panel came days after a Dallas County judge upheld a $604 million jury verdict against C.H. Robinson. The case stems from a 2021 crash in Jackson, Mississippi, that killed three people and the truck’s driver. Motor carriers ranked lawsuit abuse reform as their top concern in the American Transportation Research Institute’s 2026 Top Industry Issues report , released Oct. 18 at the conference. Lawsuit abuse reform also ranked second overall .
Marcello, who received the Trucking Associations Executive Council’s J.R. “Bob” Halladay Award in July, said fleets should treat any footage they hold as discoverable.
“If you have the activity of the driver captured by the video, you’re going to be responsible for it,” Marcello said. “And the defense or being able to say, wait, well, AI didn’t pick it up is not going to be the response. It’s not going to be an excuse.”
How AI changed camera review
Early video-based safety systems recorded an event when an accelerometer sensed G-forces past a set threshold, Ritchie said, and reviewers went through each event frame by frame. As recently as five or six years ago, he said, almost every video passed through that human layer before it reached the fleet.
Today’s cameras use computer vision trained to label risky behavior, and many send those videos straight into the fleet’s coaching workflow with no human review. Federal rules address where the camera sits: the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration ’s windshield rule allows safety technology mounted no more than 8.5 inches below the top of the area swept by the wipers. Nothing in it covers how the video is reviewed.
With no government standard for AI review, Marcello said, juries will set one. “It will be an economic governance by what you do or fail to do with that AI,” he said.
The false negatives fleets don’t see
Ritchie opened the session with a show of hands. He asked who in the room used dash cams, and every hand went up. He asked them to keep their hands up if they knew their false-positive rate, and a few dropped. Then he asked who knew their false-negative rate. Every hand went down.
A false positive flags risk that isn’t on the video. A false negative is risky behavior on the video that the AI didn’t label. Not one fleet in the room knew how often its cameras were missing it.
Solera analyzed AI-triggered videos and found up to 30% held other risk the AI didn’t flag, Ritchie said. The company hasn’t published the sample size or method behind the figure, a version of which it has cited since at least August 2025 . Ritchie said rates vary by vendor and by type of risk, and drowsy driving was the most common miss.
He tied the misses to vendors’ efforts to cut down on false alerts.
“Because these AI-only systems were getting feedback from the industry that their false positives were too high, they started to dial down the sensitivity of it,” Ritchie said. “And when they do that, you create more opportunity to have something that’s actually risky but not getting labeled as risky.”
Juries set the standard of care
A mock trial Marcello ran with a Philadelphia focus group showed how jurors judge a fleet’s follow-through. Jurors heard a hypothetical about a 35-truck carrier whose driver came over a hill, hit a line of traffic and killed two people. The driver had several overspeeds and hard brakes the week before, and the company’s lone safety director hadn’t caught up on them.
“That mock jury was totally unsympathetic,” Marcello said. “And the gist of it was, if you’re on the road, you better be paying attention.” He said the same holds for documented unsafe driving on a fleet’s video, “whether they’re picked up by AI or not.”
Marcello said cases like C.H. Robinson’s will define the standard of care one verdict at a time.
The jury in that case assigned 23% of fault to the broker and 45% to the driver, Gorgonio Gonzalez, and found Gonzalez was “subject to control by C.H. Robinson as to the details of the mission.” Marcello, who said he pulled the filings from the docket, said plaintiffs argue that finding makes Gonzalez a borrowed employee of the broker, which would combine the two shares above 50% and leave C.H. Robinson owing the full verdict.
Why unflagged video matters in court
The systemic-failure argument comes out of the reptile theory , Marcello said. He described it as “primarily a strategy for maximizing verdicts based upon engendering fear in the jury.”
“If we have a situation where there is risky behavior not caught or not flagged on the video by AI that goes uncorrected, even if that doesn’t relate to what caused the accident or what happened, it will be skewed in terms of being indicative of the lack of a safety culture and thus a systemic failure,” Marcello said.
Ritchie said fleet safety staff rarely have time to dig deeper. “Most people are wearing multiple hats,” he said. “These are very lean organizations, and they’re getting leaner by the day.” Under those conditions, he said, many safety teams are trained to coach the risk the provider labels, document it and move on to the next event. “You’re not necessarily guided to look for other things on that video that are risky,” he said. “And therein lies the problem.”
Retention policies keep that footage on hand. Ritchie said providers typically hold video with no identified risk for 30 days at most and video with any flagged risk for six months or longer, so a clip flagged for a seat belt violation can sit in the system with unflagged drowsy driving on it.
Some companies avoid analyzing their data for fear it will be discovered, a habit Marcello calls the discovery fallacy. “The fallacy is we can prevent discovery by not looking at it,” he said. “It’ll be discovered, the data itself.”
Not looking only means the plaintiff finds it first.
Three ways vendors handle review
Ritchie split vendors into three groups. Some send video from the camera straight into the fleet’s workflow, and he said those fleets need to check the footage themselves for unflagged risk. Some use human reviewers only to remove false positives. Others review for both false positives and false negatives before the video reaches the fleet.
But the argument comes from a vendor that sells human review, and neither panelist cited a court ruling that turned on an event an AI failed to flag. Marcello’s evidence was a mock jury. Ritchie also said dropping the AI wouldn’t help. Human review alone, “the old way of doing it,” is no better, he said, “just as the AI alone is not better.”
“Even though I sell AI cameras, that’s literally my job,” Ritchie said. “I feel compelled to get up here and have this conversation because I’m seeing a situation where we moved really fast, got a bunch of AI only cameras throughout the entire industry, and not one time have I heard anybody talk about a false negative. That can’t be the case anymore.”
Why it matters: Liability for what an AI camera misses stays with the fleet. Every clip a carrier stores is potential evidence, so fleets on AI-only systems inherit a review job their lean safety teams weren’t staffed for, and a jury decides what skipping it costs.

LEGO Dumps First Seven Star Wars 50th Anniversary Sets, A New Hope 3D Poster Steals the Show
31 photos
Photo: LEGO
Although to many of us alive today it may seem unbelievable, the Star Wars universe is turning half a century old next year. That’s 50 years since A New Hope came out and completely revolutionized the science fiction genre. And as you might expect, almost everyone on this planet, from Aston Martin to LEGO, is getting ready to celebrate.
We’ll be dealing with what the Danish toy maker has up its sleeve for 2027 in this story. As one of the brands most closely linked to the Star Wars franchise, there was no way in hell LEGO would have missed the moment. In fact, its 50th anniversary party starts right on January 1, 2027, when no less than seven new sets will be released.
The toys cover pretty much everything, from artwork to vehicles, and they are inspired by some of the most iconic moments in this universe. They are all accompanied by minifigures that take after, says LEGO , the original Star Wars concept art by Ralph McQuarrie, but also by reimagined collectible Star Wars poster tiles. And here they all are in all their glory, starting with my favorite.
LEGO Star Wars A New Hope Movie Poster (75467) The first movie in the franchise is what LEGO celebrates with the A New Hope Movie Poster, a 3,209-piece set that comes together to form a poster measuring over 23 inches (59 cm) high and 16 inches (40 cm) wide. It is a plastic, 3D replica of the original theatrical poster, meaning it has a lot of things to offer.
Photo: LEGO Among them, Luke Skywalker , Princess Leia, R2-D2, and C-3PO, all four set against the backdrop of Darth Vader, the Death Star, and the Battle of Yavin. The wall art can either be mounted on a wall or leaned against something, but, sadly, it doesn’t come with a support structure of its own. It does come with a collectable alternative poster tile, though.
This set, like all the others, for that matter, will be available starting January 1, 2027 (for insiders, with the rest getting access to it three days later). The poster also happens to be the most expensive of the bunch, as it will sell for $299,99.
LEGO Star Wars Upscaled Luke Skywalker (75482)
To many the main character of the first three movies in the franchise, Luke Skywalker is celebrated in this new LEGO collection with a pretty sizeable figure, measuring over ten inches (25 cm) tall and requiring the correct assembly of 981 plastic pieces.
Luke wears for the purposes of this set his his X-wing pilot uniform and helmet, and, when fully assembled, offers moveable hands, arms, legs, and head, making it ideal for posing. And he is not alone, as his sister, Princess Leia, accompanies him in minifigure form. LEGO is willing to let them both go for $99.99.
LEGO Star Wars Rebel Y-Wing Starfighter (75478) As one of the weapons platforms of the good guys in the Star Wars universe, the Y-Wing Starfighter has always been the object of desire for collectors. LEGO brings it to life in the form of a toy standing three inches (seven cm) high, 14.5 inches (37 cm) long, and seven inches (18 cm) wide. Putting it together requires 676 plastic bricks.
Photo: LEGO The spacecraft depicted here is the one seen in the Battle of Yavin, and comes complete with the minifigures of Mon Mothma, Dutch Vander, and astromech droid R2-BHD. The set comes, for $79,99, with an exclusive Luke Skywalker minifigure.
LEGO Star Wars Darth Vader 2-In-1 Wall Art (75466) Replicated in countless shapes and sizes over the past 50 years, the main antagonist of the first three Star Wars movies is celebrated by LEGO in the form of a wall art piece. Ok, technically two of them, as builders can opt for one of two displays, measuring at most ten inches (25 cm) high and just as wide.
The first is a replica of Vader’s infamous black helmet, made from 628 plastic pieces. The second shows Vader’s “I am your father” quote, using his red lightsaber as a backdrop. Completing the $69.99 set is a Star Wars: The Empire Strikes Back poster tile.
LEGO Star Wars Stormtrooper Helmet (75495) Serving the dark side while dressed in white, the fighting force of the Empire, the Stormtroopers, are celebrated by LEGO through a seven-inch (18 cm) high helmet with a design that pays tribute to the work of Ralph McQuarrie.
832 pieces of plastic are needed to form the head of the soldier with notoriously bad aim, and they are accompanied by a collectible Rogue One poster tile. The toy maker is asking $79,99 for this set, which also lands in January.
LEGO Star Wars Mustafar Duel (75470) Photo: LEGO This set brings to living rooms the moment when pre-Vader Anakin Skywalker takes on his former master and friend, Obi-Wan Kenobi. It does so with the help of two minifigures, a brick-built lava landscape, and hover pods -all of that coming to life courtesy of 372 pieces of plastic.
Accompanied by an exclusive Han Solo minifigure, this set, which stands three inches (eight cm) high and 8.5 inches (21 cm) wide, will sell right from the first day of next year for $39,99.
LEGO Star Wars Duel On Bespin (75480) Last but not least comes a set that reenacts one of the most iconic moments in Star Wars history, the fight between Luke Skywalker and Darth Vader on a bridge in Cloud City. Both characters are part of the set as minifigures, as is a printed “No, I am your father!” plaque.
The Duel on Bespin is 718 pieces strong and is accompanied by an exclusive Darth Vader minifigure, all for $79.99.

Nanning port. Credit Beibu Gulf Port Group
By Alison Koo
13 November 2026
Nanning is seeking to transform itself from an inland Chinese city into an international logistics hub serving South-east Asia, leveraging Pinglu Canal’s September opening to strengthen river-sea connectivity.
It also wants to expand trade links with the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN).
The capital of Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region is accelerating the development of an integrated transport network spanning road, rail, waterways, and air, with the canal expected to play a pivotal role in connecting inland cargo flows to international shipping routes.
Yesterday, Nanning municipal officials outlined the plans, with Municipal Bureau of Commerce deputy director Wu Shaopeng noting: “With the Pinglu Canal’s opening, Nanning port has evolved from primarily handling domestic trade into a departure point for river-sea intermodal transport.”
At the Baliang joint operation area, in the Liujing Port district, berths 1 to 6 have opened to foreign trade, allowing international cargo to be imported and exported directly through the port.
Landside logistics had also improved, said Nanning Municipal Bureau of Transportation’s director, Zhu Chao. The city’s expressway network now exceeds 1,500 km, while the Nanning International Railway Port operates daily cross-border rail freight services to Vietnam.
Mr Zhu said: “Nanning’s railway port has become China’s largest consolidation and distribution centre for rail exports to the neighbouring country.”
Air connectivity is also being expanded. Nanning Wuxu International Airport has an annual cargo and mail handling capacity of 400,000 tonnes, and operates seven international cargo routes serving ASEAN markets. It handled 127,800 tonnes of air cargo and mail between January and October, including 47,300 tonnes of international cargo.
Meanwhile, the airport’s Yong Zhi Yi (Wings of Nanning) smart air logistics platform enables transfers between international and domestic flights, cutting four hours from the time needed to distribute ASEAN-imported fruit to destinations across China.
Nanning is also seeking to improve the efficiency of cross-border cargo movements. Technical coordination for China-Vietnam cross-border express freight services has reduced station-to-station transit times between Nanning and Hanoi to as little as 14 hours.
Looking ahead, Nanning plans to increase the frequency of international freight shipping routes and cross-border rail services to ASEAN, while improving connections between rail container services, road freight, and port facilities.
Mr Zhu said: “Nanning will use the Pinglu Canal to revitalise its ports and promote coordinated development across the region. The longer-term ambition is to establish a two-way logistics corridor, facilitating exports of Chinese products to ASEAN markets through Guangxi, while providing an efficient route for South-east Asian goods entering China.”

Formula 1 Races to Have Archer Midnight VTOL Fly Air Taxi Missions for VIPs and Fans
11 photos
Photo: Archer
Slowly but surely, the world is inching toward a time when vertical take-off and landing (VTOL) aircraft will be a constant part of our lives. As if trying to get people used to the idea, Stellantis-backed VTOL maker Archer is now getting ready to unleash its MIdnight aircraft upon Formula 1 races.
Archer has been at it for years trying to make the Midnight something people routinely think about. More than a year ago, for instance, it announced that the aircraft has become the Official Air Taxi of the LA28 Olympic and Paralympic Games.
And now comes this multi-year tie-up with Formula 1. Announced this week, the partnership will see the American company deploy the Midnight at select Grand Prix events. Not all of them, thus, but only the ones that unfold in places that are of interest for the company’s future business plan, including in the U.S., Middle East, Asia and Europe.
The people who attended the United States Grand Prix in Austin, Texas, in late October got a taste of what that means, as the Midnight was on display for all to see. And so will the people who will be attending the upcoming Las Vegas Grand Prix and Abu Dhabi Grand Prix.
So, in the short run, Archer’s involvement with Formula 1 will only see the Midnight displayed on the ground. In the not-so-distant future, though, there are plans to create an air taxi service at certain Grand Prix events, so that VIPs and fans could be transported by air.
Archer is presently looking into the creation of air taxi drop-off and pick-up locations at some circuits, while Formula 1 is pondering the inclusion of these air taxi services in its hospitality and ticketing offerings. It’s unclear how long it will take until everything falls into place, but it probably won't be very long, knowing Formula 1’s affinity to lead the way.
The only thing standing in the way of that happening right now is the fact that the Midnight, like most other VTOL designs out there, is not yet fully operational and cleared to fly in the sky for commercial purposes.
When it does get the green light, the VTOL will fly as many as four people at a time, transporting them to maximum distances of 100 miles (160 km) on a single charge of its batteries. The maximum speed the design is capable of reaching is 150 mph (241 kph).
The company is presently in the process of testing the Midnight under the U.S. government’s VTOL Integration Pilot Program (eIPP), and it plans to soon start operating the aircraft commercially. Alongside it, so will air carriers such as United Airlines, Ethiopian Airlines, and Abu Dhabi Aviation, which have already expressed interest in the design. And so did the U.S. Air Force, for that matter.

Theon Design Unveils New Bespoke Porsche 911 Build, Rocks F1-Grade Carbon Fiber and 419 HP
65 photos
Photo: Theon Design
It took 18 months for this collaboration to take shape in the form of a gorgeous bespoke air-cooled 911, but judging by the results, I'd say it was worth the wait. You're looking at a 419-hp 4.0L coupe with an Oak Green Neo Metallic finish and a total weight of just 1,150 kg (2,535 lbs). That's 364 hp per metric ton.
This thing also packs selectable engine maps and a G50 five-speed manual gearbox, while the previously-mentioned semi-active dampers, bespoke spring rates, and wheels all combine to offer more precise handling and better ride compliance. Way better for UK roads than stock.
In terms of construction, the car's exterior bodywork, bumper and lower sill panels are all formed from carbon fiber, and this includes various trim panels. Altogether, we're talking about a roughly 300 kg (661 lbs) weight loss regimen.
Visually, I already mentioned the Oak Green Neo Metallic (an updated version of the classic Oak Green Metallic), but not how well it's complemented by the champagne Porsche script and matching exterior details. Even the wheels are rocking this hue - as are the brake discs and calipers.
Meanwhile, the 4.0L engine also produces 322 lb-ft (437 Nm) of torque, which may not sound like a lot, but trust me, it's enough for something that weighs this little. According to Theon Design , this car can accelerate from zero to 60 mph (97 kph) in about 4 seconds flat. That's air-cooled heaven right there.
Moving along to the interior, highlights include the Beechwood semi-aniline and nubuck leather upholstery, champagne detailing, Recaro CS seats, new window switches, a fully electric heating and air-conditioning system, and more.
"As with every commission Theon Design undertakes, this project began by listening to what the client wanted – not just how they wanted their car to look, but how they wanted it to feel. That informed every aspect of the development program, from the engine, transmission, and brake package to spring rates, damper calibration, and steering response," stated Theon Design co-founder, Adam Hawley.
Photo: Theon Design "Throughout the eighteen-month development period, we spoke regularly with the client, involving them in all the decisions that would affect the car’s character. From the first conversation to the final sign-off drive, collaboration is key and ensures that the ownership experience is every bit as personal and rewarding as the design."
All this sounds pretty good, right? Well, something even more special is taking shape in the upcoming Theon R - meant to be the company's most hardcore interpretation of the air-cooled 911 . It'll put down over 500 hp while utilizing motorsport-derived technology and weighing less than 1,000 kg (2,200 lbs). It should make for an amazing driver's car, so stay tuned!
But what do you guys think? Would you rather drive a custom air-cooled 911 on the weekends, or something a little more... substantial ?

By Gavin van Marle
13 November 2026
Container spot freight rates on the transpacific and Asia-Europe trades saw another week of gentle declines amid reduced demand post-peak season, while Asia-Europe carriers and their customers begin annual contract negotiations in earnest.
This week’s World Container Index (WCI) from Drewry saw spot rates on its Shanghai-Rotterdam leg decline 3% week on week, to $3,504 per 40ft, while pricing on the Shanghai-Genoa route remained flat for the third week in a row, at $4,168 per 40ft.
A new round of FAK (freight all kinds) levels are set to be applied next week, although they are modest in ambition and generally range from $4,500-$5,000 per 40ft on Asia-North Europe shipments, and between $5,500-$6,600 per 40ft on Asia-Mediterranean. They are largely around the level carriers have been targeting for the past couple of months.
However, they are also being accompanied by increased number of blanked sailings – according to Drewry’s Container Capacity Insight, eight are scheduled for next week, compared with the five this week.
The key aspect to this is that carriers and their customers are positioning for next year, with carriers keen to get spot rates up as much as they can to act as a guide for contract rates, and shippers are, understandably, eager for them to be suppressed after enduring a wild ride during much of 2026.
“Those conversations are starting more or less as we speak,” Hapag-Lloyd chief executive Rolf Habben Jansen told analysts at the line’s third-quarters earnings call this week.
“As is usual at this time of year, not everybody sees the market the same – I think when one looks at contracts that will be closed for 2027, they will be at a higher level than what we have seen in 2026.
“Also, when you take out the bunker component, that alone will push rates up, of course. But I think we will also see a fairly significant net increase of freight rates going into 2027,” he added.
Much will therefore depend on the stickiness of pre-Chinese New Year peak season surcharges (PSSs) that are on their way for the beginning of December. Maersk has announced a $1,000 per 40ft PSS on Asia-North Europe shipments from 1 December, while CMA CGM is going earlier, with a $1,600 per 40ft PSS for Asia-Mediterranean shipments due on 25 November.
While some Loadstar sources expressed surprise at the early timing, given that the Chinese New Year (CNY) holiday begins on 6 February, Vespucci Maritime founder Lars Jensen noted it was probably appropriate, given that peak pre-CNY demand will occupy most of January.
On the transpacific trades, rates have finally began to properly descend after remaining elevated throughout October.
The WCI’s Shanghai-Los Angeles route was down 2% on the previous week, to end at $7,416 per 40ft, while its Shanghai-New York leg declined 3%, to $9,020 per 40ft container, its lowest since August.
However, forwarders on the trade said widespread discounts had been available this week, and virtually no cargo had been booked at published rate levels.
“Instead, actual moving rates are dictated by carrier promotional discounts and volume-based pricing, as space across Asian origin ports continues to open up,” said US west coast forwarder Freight Right.
Carriers have responded to the slowdown in demand with more blanked sailings – eight transpacific voyages will be blanked next week, compared with four this week, according to Drewry – and Freight Right said shippers should be aware that the cheapest spot rates could come with poor reliability for the remainder of the year.
“Ocean freight activity is expected to slow further through late November and December, supporting a broadly-stable-to-gradually-softer rate outlook.
“Improved space availability should give importers more booking flexibility, although the lowest price may come with greater schedule uncertainty,” it said.

Mysterious Off-Road-Ready Test Mule Spied, Could It Be Audi’s Mercedes G-Class Rival?
10 photos
Photo: SH Proshots
While the Volkswagen Group is struggling financially and some upcoming products have been put on ice for now, the automotive giant appears to be preparing a very interesting vehicle as we speak, and if it is indeed what we said in the title, then it will be one very special ride.
First things first, these images just ended up in our inboxes sent by our spy photographers, who immortalized this mysterious test mule somewhere in Europe, at an Audi facility. The location is said to be “extremely confidential and sensitive,” which is why they have removed the background in order to “protect the exact location and our sources.” And now you know why this thing appears to be floating in the air next to a leafless tree.
Our man with the cam also noted that the camouflage is not typical for Audi , but then again, this is no ordinary machine either. It has been clearly built for some serious off-roading, hence the large ground clearance, and the six-lug wheels shod in BFGoodrich all-terrain tires. It has a light bar on the roof, some sturdy side steps, fender flares, and this is basically where everything that we know about it ends and the speculation begins.
Thus, as we said in the title, there is a chance that we are indeed looking at Audi’s rival to the likes of the Mercedes G-Wagen. This thing has been brought into discussion for the past couple of years or so, though it seems that it was eventually forgotten. To be honest, this might not be a great time to develop such a thing, as it definitely eats a huge amount of money poured into the research and development, and not only, but it appears to be a bet that the four-ring brand has already placed.
Photo: SH Proshots Mind you, there is no clear indication that we are indeed looking at the Mercedes G-Class rival from Audi , as even our spies are not entirely convinced. In fact, they have said that it could be a test mule of the future Volkswagen Touareg, too. However, we wouldn’t bet on it, because the six-lug wheels do not seem like a logical approach for such a thing. Then again, they definitely fit the nature of a real off-road from Audi.
Audi themselves, through the voice of CEO Gernot Dollner, suggested that the SUV in question might share quite a few things with Scout’s new models, namely the Terra and the Traveler. The latter is an SUV, whereas the former is a pickup. And guess what? Both feature six-lug wheels, just like this mysterious tester that recently became the focus of our spy photographer’s camera lens.
The company’s head honcho said that a body-on-frame SUV is “ in the framework, ” although he admitted that “ no decision has been taken yet, ” adding that “ if we do something like that, it is only thinkable to do it on a platform that is already there. ” Scout’s Terra and Traveler were unveiled in the United States of America last year, and will be put together locally starting from 2027.
If you think that Audi’s potential upcoming G-Wagen rival might be offered with gasoline power, perhaps with a V8 being part of the offering, then you are wrong. That’s because the Scout models are fully electric, with dual-motor setups and full-time four-wheel drive. Moreover, they also feature a ladder-frame construction, as well as locking differentials at the front and rear.
Photo: SH Proshots However, given that EVs are not exactly popular in some parts of the world, we would not be surprised to learn that Audi might shift its strategy when it comes to the Mercedes G-Wagen competitor . And if that happens, then it will be interesting to learn whether the platform might be modified to support ICE power. If the answer is yes, then there is a chance that the Scouts might also get ICE units, though this is pure speculation at this point, so you may want to take it with a pinch of salt.
By the way, let’s not forget that the Mercedes G-Wagen also comes with EV power. The model is called the Mercedes-Benz G 580, features four permanently synchronous electric motors, has 579 hp (432 kW/587 ps) and 859 pound-feet (1,165 Nm) of torque in total, and completes the 0-60 mph (0-97 kph) in 4.6 seconds. And it’s not exactly that popular, in case you forgot.
It’s not only the Mercedes-Benz G-Class and its range-topping version, the Mercedes- AMG G 63, that will be targeted by the Audi off-roader, but also the Land Rover Defender. BMW is also reportedly working on such a thing. The project is codenamed the G74, and could be a bit milder, as it is expected to utilize the versatile CLAR construction, albeit perhaps with a few modifications.
What’s your take on the fact that Audi and BMW are both interested in launching some off-road-oriented models? And could this test mule actually offer an initial glimpse into the four-ring brand’s upcoming 4x4?
